chunks: Al-Saffar from Muhammad ibn Isa from Ja'far ibn Isa said:

I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), 'May I be your ransom, goods are sold, and the caller calls out on them. When he calls out on them, he is free from every defect in them. When the buyer buys it and is satisfied with it, and only the payment of the price remains, perhaps he becomes indifferent (to it). When he becomes indifferent to it, he claims defects in it and that he did not know of them. So the caller says to him, 'I have freed myself from them.' And the buyer says to him, 'I did not hear the freeing from them.' Is he believed so that the price is not obligatory upon him, or is he not believed so that the price is obligatory upon him?' He (peace be upon him) wrote back, 'The price is obligatory upon him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a buyer claims defects in a purchased item after the seller has announced freedom from defects?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Rida (AS) clarifies the evidentiary weight of the seller's public declaration of 'baraa' (release from defects) during auction or sale processes. In Shia jurisprudence, this establishes that the buyer's failure to hear the announcement does not invalidate the seller's claim, thereby protecting the seller from post-transaction disputes over hidden defects. It underscores the principle of 'bayyinah' (proof) resting on the seller's explicit statement, reinforcing commercial certainty in market transactions.
